description:
Wesam Saad examines the tribulation's midpoint and worship under the beast through Matthew 24, Daniel and Revelation 11–13. He connects the abomination of desolation with intensified persecution and compares the three-and-a-half-year descriptions with forty-two months and 1,260 days. The two witnesses continue to proclaim their message during the period he describes. In Revelation 12's sign, he identifies the woman with Israel, the child with Christ and the dragon with Satan, using Joseph's dream as background. He distinguishes the heavenly conflict and Satan's expulsion from the earthly persecution that follows in his interpretation.

Questions clarify the beast, false prophet and dragon as distinct figures and explore how power, deception and coercion work together. Saad treats willing worship as central to the mark and rejects automatically equating ordinary present technology with that future allegiance. His conclusions about irreversible worship and the book of life include expressly tentative reasoning. The beast's wound, apparent recovery and possible technological explanations remain unresolved rather than a forecast about a device. The session also announces the planned Heaven study using Randy Alcorn's book, before the course returns to eternal rewards. This explicit outline links the coming Heaven material to the same End Times course. Throughout, Saad's distinctions call for attention to what is stated and what remains interpretation or speculation.

questions.question: How does Saad connect the midpoint with intensified tribulation?
questions.answer: He links Daniel's covenant language and the abomination of desolation with Jesus' instruction to flee in Matthew 24. He understands the latter half of the period as an intensification of the tribulation, rather than the beginning of all divine wrath. The exact alignment of events is his synthesis of the passages.

questions.question: How does he relate the different time expressions?
questions.answer: Saad connects forty-two months and 1,260 days with three-and-a-half years. He uses these expressions to organise the holy city's oppression, the witnesses' ministry and the period of intensified persecution in his reading.

questions.question: How does he identify the woman, child and dragon?
questions.answer: Saad reads the vision as an explicitly signalled symbol. He identifies the woman as Israel through the sun, moon and stars associated with Joseph's dream, the child as Christ and the dragon as Satan. Those identifications express his interpretation of the sign, not a claim that a literal dragon pursues a literal woman.

questions.question: How does he relate the war in heaven to events on earth?
questions.answer: He reads Satan's expulsion as a cause of intensified earthly persecution and connects the dragon's authority with the beast's actions. When asked about Daniel, he does not confidently identify another reference and distinguishes the earlier angelic conflict mentioned by a participant from this future scene.

questions.question: What purpose does he assign to the two witnesses?
questions.answer: Saad describes a protected ministry that confronts hostility while calling people to repentance and faith. Their presence means the period is not presented as entirely without gospel proclamation, even while he expects increasing persecution.

questions.question: Are the beast, false prophet and dragon one figure?
questions.answer: No. The questions lead Saad to distinguish the dragon as Satan, the beast as the Antichrist and the false prophet as the figure who directs people towards beast worship. His false-trinity comparison is an analogy for their coordinated roles, not a claim that they share divine nature.

questions.question: How certain is his conclusion about beast worship and the book of life?
questions.answer: Saad reasons that willful worship reveals a settled rejection and an absence from the book of life, repeatedly using tentative language. He also allows that some people who are not yet believers may refuse beast worship and later believe. His argument must not become a verdict about a named present-day person.

questions.question: Does he identify the mark with ordinary present-day chips or barcodes?
questions.answer: No. He locates it within the future worship-and-coercion setting and says an ordinary chip now is not inherently the mark or a sin. He speculates about possible workarounds but does not establish their reality or supply a settled account; the generated study does not turn that speculation into instructions.

questions.question: What can be concluded about the beast's wound and recovery?
questions.answer: Saad discusses a fatal wound and an apparent return that deceives observers, while also denying Satan the power of true resurrection. He offers possible explanations but acknowledges they are unknown. Robotics, AI or later technology therefore remain hypothetical mechanisms, not verified prophecy or a resolved explanation.

questions.question: How does the closing outline connect this teaching with the Heaven studies?
questions.answer: Saad announces the bowls and return of Christ before a sustained study of the new earth, using Randy Alcorn's Heaven as a discussion framework. He still intends eternal rewards as the later practical culmination. This establishes continuity through an explicit course plan, rather than similar subject matter alone.
